propositions.text: Two appeals concern validity of decisions by Montreal Port Authority and CBC on PILTs to City of Montréal.
propositions.quote: These two appeals concern the validity of decisions made by two federal Crown corporations, the Montreal Port Authority (“MPA”) and the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (“CBC”), regarding the calculation of the payments in lieu of real property taxes (“PILTs”) they make to the City of Montréal.

propositions.text: Decisions were unreasonable; appeals allowed; Federal Court of Appeal judgments dismissed; Federal Court judgments restored.
propositions.quote: For the reasons that follow, I find that those decisions were unreasonable. I would therefore allow the appeals, set aside the judgments of the Federal Court of Appeal dismissing the City’s applications for judicial review, and restore the Federal Court’s judgments quashing the respondents’ decisions.

propositions.text: CBC’s cross-appeal on PILT calculation basis dismissed.
propositions.quote: I would also dismiss the CBC’s cross‑appeal concerning the basis adopted by the Federal Court of Appeal for calculating its PILTs.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds MPA and CBC decisions on PILTs unreasonable, allows appeals, restores Federal Court judgments, and dismisses CBC's cross-appeal.

propositions.text: Appeals arise from municipal amalgamations on Montréal island starting in 2000, combining most municipalities into City of Montréal and restructuring municipal taxation.
propositions.quote: These appeals arise out of the municipal amalgamations that took place on the island of Montréal starting in 2000. Following a series of events that I will not discuss, those amalgamations combined most of the municipalities on the island into the City of Montréal. They also resulted in a major restructuring of Montréal’s municipal taxation system.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states appeals arise from 2000 municipal amalgamations on Montréal island and taxation restructuring.

propositions.text: Before 2003, City collected property taxes plus surtax on non-residential immovables and occupancy tax on commercial premises in some municipalities.
propositions.quote: Before 2003, the City of Montréal collected property taxes on all taxable immovables within its territory. To the general property tax, it added a surtax on non‑residential immovables. It also imposed an occupancy tax on commercial and professional premises. However, that business tax was imposed prior to the amalgamations in only 10 of the 28 municipalities that were to become part of the City.

propositions.text: City abolished business tax in 2003, changed property tax to recover lost amounts, created variable property tax rates by use classification.
propositions.quote: As authorized by provincial legislation, the City abolished the business tax effective at the start of the 2003 fiscal year. It changed its property tax to recover the amounts it would lose after abolishing the business tax. It created a property tax system under which rates varied depending on the purposes for which immovables were used. Immovables classified as non‑residential were subject to a property tax rate that was calculated using variable rates based on the classification of property.

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains City abolished business tax in 2003 and changed property tax rates by use classification.

propositions.text: In 2003 and after, City asked MPA and CBC to pay PILTs using non-residential rates; respondents refused amounts claimed.
propositions.quote: In 2003 and the following years, the City asked the MPA and the CBC to make PILTs calculated using one of the rates applicable to non‑residential immovables. The respondents refused to pay the amounts claimed by the City.

propositions.text: PILT Act required respondents to pay PILTs as Crown corporations; previously they paid property tax but no PILTs for business tax.
propositions.quote: The Payments in Lieu of Taxes Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. M‑13 (“PILT Act ”), required them to make PILTs because of their status as Crown corporations. Until that time, they had made payments corresponding to the property tax on the taxable value of the immovables they owned in Montréal but had made no PILTs in respect of the business tax.

propositions.text: Changes to property tax increased payments requested by City; MPA reduced payment by amount related to abolished business tax and excluded silos and piers from PILT basis.
propositions.quote: The changes made to the property tax significantly increased the payments requested by the City (2008 FCA 278, 389 N.R. 305, at para. 16, per Létourneau J.A.). The MPA decided to reduce its payment in lieu by an amount equivalent to the portion of the property tax increase that resulted from the abolition of the business tax, and to exclude the value of silos and piers at the port of Montréal from the basis for calculating its PILTs.

propositions.text: MPA considered silos and piers not immovables for PILTs; CBC excluded business tax recovery amounts and used residual property tax rate, claimed compensation rights.
propositions.quote: In its opinion, the silos and piers were not immovables in respect of which it had to make PILTs. The CBC excluded the amounts corresponding to the City’s recovery of the proceeds of the abolished business tax and calculated a PILT based on Montréal’s tax rate for the residual category of property, that is, 1.9522% in 2003 rather than the 4.1722% claimed by the City. It also maintained that it was entitled to effect compensation between its PILTs and amounts the City of Montréal owed it for overpayments.

propositions.text: City disagreed and applied to Federal Court for judicial review under Federal Courts Act, arguing respondents’ decisions unlawful and unreasonable.
propositions.quote: The City disagreed with those decisions and challenged them by applying to the Federal Court for judicial review under ss. 18 and 18.1 of the Federal Courts Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F‑7 . It argued that the respondents’ decisions were unlawful and unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The Court describes City’s PILT claims, respondents’ refusals, and City’s judicial review applications.

propositions.text: Martineau J. allowed City’s judicial review applications, quashed respondents’ PILT calculation decisions, except excluding piers but not silos for MPA.
propositions.quote: Martineau J. allowed the appellant’s applications for judicial review and quashed the respondents’ decisions concerning the calculation of their PILTs (2007 FC 700, 314 F.T.R. 226, and 2007 FC 701, 61 R.P.R. (4th) 168). He did rule in the MPA’s favour on excluding the piers from the basis for calculating its PILTs, but not on excluding the silos.

paragraphs.summary: The Federal Court judge allowed City’s judicial review, quashing respondents’ decisions except excluding piers for MPA.

propositions.text: Martineau J. applied pre-Dunsmuir and Khosa case law, using correctness standard of review.
propositions.quote: Martineau J. applied the case law on judicial review as it stood prior to Dunsmuir and Khosa (Dunsmuir v. New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9, [2008] 1 S.C.R. 190; Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v. Khosa, 2009 SCC 12, [2009] 1 S.C.R. 339). In his opinion, the relevant standard of review was correctness.

propositions.text: Respondents’ decisions were arbitrary, capricious, and made without jurisdiction; discretion did not allow disregarding general tax rate for non-residential immovables.
propositions.quote: Applying that standard, he found that the respondents’ decisions were arbitrary and capricious and had even been made without jurisdiction. He noted that the increase in the property tax rate did not change the nature of the tax. The discretion given to Crown corporations to set the appropriate rate when calculating PILTs did not authorize them to disregard the tax rate generally applicable to owners of non‑residential immovables in the municipality.

propositions.text: Silos were not exempt federal property and had to be included in MPA’s PILT calculation; piers excluded.
propositions.quote: In the MPA’s case, Martineau J. also found that the silos were not exempt federal property and that they had to be considered in calculating its PILTs, but he excluded the piers from this calculation.

paragraphs.summary: The Federal Court judge found respondents’ decisions arbitrary, lacking jurisdiction, and ruled on silos and piers inclusion.

propositions.text: Matineau J. referred matters back to respondents to set PILTs for 2003 and 2004 using effective rates applicable to their property classification; no deduction for abolished business tax.
propositions.quote: Martineau J. referred the matters back to the respondents to have them set their PILTs for 2003 and 2004 on the basis of effective rates corresponding to the tax rates applicable to their property as classified. He added that the MPA and the CBC could not deduct the equivalent of the business tax abolished by the City of Montréal in making their calculations.

propositions.text: Respondents appealed to Federal Court of Appeal.
propositions.quote: The respondents appealed that judgment to the Federal Court of Appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The Federal Court judge remitted PILT calculations to respondents and noted no deduction for abolished business tax; respondents appealed.

propositions.text: Federal Court of Appeal set aside Federal Court decisions, dismissed City’s judicial review applications, applying correctness standard.
propositions.quote: Létourneau J.A., writing for a unanimous Court of Appeal, intervened, setting aside the Federal Court’s decisions and dismissing the City’s applications for judicial review (2008 FCA 278, 389 N.R. 305). He applied the standard of correctness to determine whether the respondents had an administrative discretion in setting the amounts of their PILTs.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal found respondents had discretion and exercised it reasonably; decisions consistent with PILT Act purpose and Parliament’s intent.
propositions.quote: He found that they did have such a discretion and that they had exercised it reasonably. In his opinion, the impugned decisions were consistent with the purpose and the general scheme of the PILT Act and with Parliament’s intent.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal corrected CBC’s tax rate used, ruling CBC’s PILTs must be calculated like MPA’s.
propositions.quote: However, he corrected the tax rate used by the CBC, which was actually the rate for residential immovables consisting of fewer than six dwellings. He held that the use of that rate was unjustified and that the CBC’s PILTs had to be calculated in the same manner as the MPA’s.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal ruled silos excluded from MPA’s PILT calculation.
propositions.quote: He ruled in the MPA’s favour with regard to the silos and held that they were not to be included in the calculation of its PILTs.

paragraphs.summary: The Federal Court of Appeal reversed Federal Court, found respondents’ discretion reasonable, corrected CBC’s rate, and excluded silos for MPA.

propositions.text: Appellant asks Court to restore Federal Court decisions.
propositions.quote: In these appeals, the appellant asks that the decisions of Martineau J. be restored.

propositions.text: CBC cross-appeals to vary Federal Court of Appeal judgment, seeking to use residential tax rate for PILTs.
propositions.quote: The CBC, in its cross‑appeal, asks this Court to vary in part the judgment of the Federal Court of Appeal by authorizing the CBC to return to its original basis for calculating its PILTs, that is, using the tax rate for residential immovables consisting of fewer than six dwellings, which was the residual rate provided for in the City of Montréal’s by‑laws.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant seeks restoration of Federal Court decisions; CBC cross-appeals to use residential tax rate for PILTs.

propositions.text: Appellant argues PILT Act regulations unlawfully delegate Governor in Council’s regulatory powers; no need to consider as validity not challenged.
propositions.quote: The appellant makes various arguments in support of its appeals. In particular, it submits that the regulations made under the PILT Act include an unlawful delegation of the regulatory powers conferred on the Governor in Council. There is no need to consider this argument, since the validity of the regulations has not been challenged and since the instant cases can be decided without considering it.

propositions.text: CBC argues it may effect compensation between PILTs and overpayments; no need to consider this issue here.
propositions.quote: The CBC submits that it may effect compensation between its PILTs and overpayments allegedly collected by the City. As will be seen, there is no need to consider this issue in the context of these appeals.

propositions.text: Court will limit analysis to issues bearing on case outcome.
propositions.quote: I will limit my analysis to the issues that actually have a bearing on the outcome of these cases.

paragraphs.summary: Appellant and CBC raise arguments not considered; Court limits analysis to outcome-relevant issues.

propositions.text: Proceedings are judicial review applications; Court must identify standard of review for impugned decisions.
propositions.quote: To begin with, the nature of the proceedings brought by the appellant must be borne in mind. As they are applications for judicial review, I must identify the standard of review to be applied in reviewing the impugned decisions to determine whether they are valid.

propositions.text: Court will consider PILT system, legal nature, Crown corporations’ powers, municipal taxation development, and Montréal’s tax reform.
propositions.quote: For that purpose, I will consider the system for setting PILTs, the legal nature of PILTs, and the powers conferred on Crown corporations and administrators of federal property for determining what amounts should be paid. I will also summarize the development of municipal taxation in Quebec and discuss the reform by the City of Montréal of the taxation system applicable within its territory.

propositions.text: Analysis prefaced by review of constitutional principles on immunity from taxation of federal and provincial governments.
propositions.quote: However, this analysis must be prefaced by a brief review of the constitutional principles relating to the immunity from taxation of the federal and provincial governments in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The Court outlines its approach to judicial review, including PILT system, taxation history, and constitutional immunity principles.

propositions.text: Section 125 of Constitution Act, 1867 provides federal and provincial government property immune from taxation by other level of government.
propositions.quote: Section 125 of the Constitution Act, 1867 provides that property of the Government of Canada or a provincial government is not liable to taxation by the other level of government.

propositions.text: Proper federal system functioning requires each government respect other’s immunity from taxation (Westbank First Nation case).
propositions.quote: The proper functioning of the federal system requires that each level of government respect the other’s immunity from taxation (Westbank First Nation v. British Columbia Hydro and Power Authority, [1999] 3 S.C.R. 134, at paras. 4 and 17).

paragraphs.summary: The Court states constitutional immunity from taxation of federal and provincial government property and cites Westbank First Nation case.

propositions.text: Federal government aware its property is part of provincial and municipal fabric and receives municipal services beyond goods supply.
propositions.quote: Despite the importance of this principle, however, the federal government was of course aware that its property forms part of the territorial fabric of the provinces and municipalities. As owners of real property, the federal government and its agents receive a range of municipal services that go well beyond the mere supply of goods like water or electricity.

paragraphs.summary: The Court notes federal property receives municipal services beyond goods supply.

propositions.text: Federal government created system to compensate municipalities, encouraging federal agents to act as good residents.
propositions.quote: For this reason, the federal government created a system to compensate Canadian municipalities. In short, it wanted its administrators and agents to act as good residents of the municipalities where federal property is located.

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains federal government created compensation system for municipalities to encourage good residency.

propositions.text: Federal government established payments in lieu system; municipalities cannot sue Crown but can seek judicial review of payment decisions.
propositions.quote: To ensure that this was done, the federal government gradually established a system of payments to be made in lieu of the taxes Canadian municipalities generally collect from their ratepayers. Under this system, municipalities cannot sue the federal Crown or its agents to collect municipal taxes or PILTs. However, they can contest decisions by the federal Crown or its agents regarding the amounts to be paid by bringing the appropriate proceeding in the proper forum, that is, by applying to the Federal Court for judicial review.

propositions.text: Issue is whether PILT rules have been interpreted and applied to create basis for judicial review application.
propositions.quote: Thus, the issue is whether the rules governing PILTs have been interpreted and applied in such a way as to create a basis for an application for judicial review.

propositions.text: Appeals before Court originated in judicial review proceedings, not tax recovery actions.
propositions.quote: The appeals now before this Court originated in such a proceeding, not in an action to recover taxes.

propositions.text: Court will now examine statutory and regulatory scheme structuring payments in lieu system.
propositions.quote: I will therefore turn now to the statutory and regulatory scheme that structures the system of payments in lieu in issue here.

paragraphs.summary: The Court describes PILT system, municipalities’ inability to sue Crown, judicial review process, and frames issue for review.

propositions.text: Development of current system began in 1950 with Municipal Grants Regulations under 1949 Appropriation Act.
propositions.quote: The development of the current system began in 1950. Regulations concerning municipal grants established an initial legal framework for voluntary payments by the federal government to municipalities (The Municipal Grants Regulations, SOR/50‑54). Those regulations were made under the 1949 appropriation Act (The Appropriation Act, No. 7, 1949, S.C. 1949, c. 42).

propositions.text: 1951 Municipal Grants Act made Minister of Finance responsible for determining accepted value of federal property and grant amounts.
propositions.quote: In 1951, Parliament passed legislation that included the provisions of the Municipal Grants Regulations of 1950 (The Municipal Grants Act, S.C. 1951, c. 54). Under this Act , the Minister of Finance of Canada was responsible for determining the “accepted” value of federal property and the amount of the grants to be paid (ss. 2 and 4 ).

propositions.text: 1957 amendments introduced calculation methods including 'effective rate' defined as rate Minister considers applicable if property were taxable.
propositions.quote: In 1957, the 1951 Act was amended to introduce methods for calculating the grants that would subsequently be included in the statute and regulations in force today. The amendments introduced, in particular, the concept of the “effective rate” of tax, which the Minister was to use in calculating the grants to be paid in lieu of taxes (An Act to amend the Municipal Grants Act, S.C. 1957, c. 10). Moreover, that the Minister would have a discretion in fixing the effective rate was recognized in the very definition of the term: “effective rate” was defined in the Act as “. . . the rate of tax that, in the opinion of the Minister, would be applicable to any federal property in a municipality if that property were taxable property” (s. 1 ).

paragraphs.summary: The Court outlines historical development of PILT system from 1950 regulations to 1957 amendments introducing effective tax rate concept.

propositions.text: 1967 federal Cabinet directive asked Crown corporations to pay municipal grants consistent with Municipal Grants Act principles, acknowledging discretion.
propositions.quote: In 1967, a federal Cabinet directive asked Crown corporations to pay municipal grants on a basis consistent with the principles established in the Municipal Grants Act (Record of Cabinet Decision, March 21, 1967, A.R. No. 32881, vol. 5, at p. 94). In the directive, it was acknowledged that Crown corporations should retain some discretion in calculating their payments.

paragraphs.summary: The Court notes 1967 Cabinet directive requiring Crown corporations to pay municipal grants with discretion.

propositions.text: Legal framework for payments in lieu amended several times; statute and regulations applicable here enacted in early 2000s.
propositions.quote: The legal framework for payments in lieu has since been amended several times. The statute applicable to the instant cases was enacted and the applicable regulations made in the early 2000s. I will discuss them now.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states the legal framework was amended multiple times, with current statute and regulations from early 2000s.

propositions.text: PILT Act applies to payments for departmental federal property; regulations apply to Crown corporations and agents’ payments.
propositions.quote: There are two aspects to the statutory and regulatory scheme established by the Government of Canada for payments in lieu. On the one hand, the PILT Act, as amended by the Act to amend the Municipal Grants Act, S.C. 2000, c. 8, applies to payments in respect of “departmental” property owned directly by the federal Crown and to the calculation of those payments. On the other hand, the same Act provides that regulations may be made respecting payments in lieu by Crown corporations and agents of the Crown. Such regulations have been made, and they apply in the instant cases (Crown Corporation Payments Regulations, SOR/81‑1030 (“Regulations”), as amended by SOR/2001‑494).

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains PILT Act covers departmental property payments; regulations cover Crown corporations’ payments, applicable here.

propositions.text: PILT Act upholds federal Crown property immunity from taxation; no right to payment conferred by Act.
propositions.quote: It is clear from the PILT Act that Parliament intended to uphold the immunity of federal Crown property from taxation. Section 15 of the Act provides that “[n]o right to a payment is conferred by this Act .”

propositions.text: PILT Act establishes system balancing tax fairness for municipalities and constitutional immunity, retaining structured administrative discretion in payment amounts.
propositions.quote: Parliament therefore did not intend to give municipalities the status of creditors of the Crown for payments in lieu of taxes. Instead, it has, through the PILT Act, established a system in which municipalities expect to receive payments but the payments are made within the statutory and regulatory framework that Parliament established without renouncing the principle of immunity from taxation. Thus, the PILT Act is designed to reconcile different objectives — tax fairness for municipalities and the preservation of constitutional immunity from taxation — that can be attained only by retaining a structured administrative discretion where the setting of the amounts of payments in lieu is concerned.

propositions.text: PILT Act defines relationship between payment system and provincial/municipal tax systems which vary across Canada.
propositions.quote: For the purpose of establishing those amounts, the PILT Act must define the relationship between the system for setting payments in lieu, on the one hand, and the provincial and municipal tax systems, which can vary from place to place in Canada, on the other.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states PILT Act preserves Crown immunity, balances tax fairness, and defines relationship with provincial and municipal tax systems.

propositions.text: The PILT Act establishes a voluntary compensation system in lieu of municipal taxes for Crown property and Crown corporations.
propositions.quote: The PILT Act establishes a system for compensation to be paid in lieu of municipal taxes, but those payments do not constitute debts to the provinces or municipalities.

propositions.text: The PILT Act applies to Crown and Crown corporation property and confirms payments in lieu of real property, frontage, area, and business occupancy taxes.
propositions.quote: The PILT Act applies to property of the Crown and of Crown corporations (s. 2). It confirms the principle that amounts are to be paid in lieu of real property taxes, frontage or area taxes, and business occupancy taxes.

propositions.text: Real property tax is defined as a tax levied by a taxing authority on owners or lessees, computed by applying a rate to assessed value.
propositions.quote: The term “real property tax” is defined as follows in s. 2 of the PILT Act: a tax of general application to real property or immovables or any class of them that is (a) levied by a taxing authority on owners of real property or immovables or, if the owner is exempt from the tax, on lessees or occupiers of real property or immovables, other than those lessees or occupiers exempt by law, and (b) computed by applying a rate to all or part of the assessed value of taxable property; . . .

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains the PILT Act's voluntary compensation system for Crown property taxes and defines real property tax under the Act.

propositions.text: A taxing authority is defined as any municipal or provincial body levying real property tax under provincial law.
propositions.quote: The reference point used in the PILT Act is the real property tax established by a “taxing authority”, which is defined in s. 2 as “(a) any municipality, province, municipal or provincial board, commission, corporation or other authority that levies and collects a real property tax . . . pursuant to an Act of the legislature of a province”.

propositions.text: Payment in lieu equals the effective tax rate times the property value, both defined by the Minister's opinion.
propositions.quote: According to the PILT Act, a payment in lieu corresponds to the product of the effective rate applicable to the federal property in the taxation year and the property value of the property (s. 4(1) ).

propositions.text: The Minister has discretion to determine property value and effective rate for payment calculations under the PILT Act.
propositions.quote: The PILT Act thus confers on the Minister a discretion to be exercised in determining the property value that will apply in calculating payments in lieu.

propositions.text: Certain federal properties, including reservoirs, are excluded from payment calculations under Schedule II item 10 of the PILT Act.
propositions.quote: Moreover, s. 2(3) excludes a long and varied list of federal properties from the basis for computing the payment amounts. In particular, item 10 of Schedule II to the PILT Act excludes reservoirs and certain other facilities.

propositions.text: The MPA argues that port silos qualify as reservoirs and should be excluded from payment calculations.
propositions.quote: The MPA argues that the silos at the port of Montréal can be considered reservoirs for the purposes of that provision.

propositions.text: The Minister is authorized to make payments consistent with the PILT Act framework.
propositions.quote: The Minister is authorized to make payments that are consistent with this legal framework (s. 3(1) ).

propositions.text: An advisory panel resolves disputes over property value or effective rate, excluding judicial or administrative authorities under provincial law.
propositions.quote: The PILT Act establishes an advisory panel that is responsible for advising the Minister on the settlement of any dispute with a taxing authority over the property value or effective rate of tax applicable to any property (s. 11.1 ). Such disputes are not within the jurisdiction of the judicial or administrative authorities that would be responsible for settling them under the relevant provincial law.

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains definitions, Minister's discretion, exclusions, and dispute resolution under the PILT Act, noting MPA's argument about silos.

propositions.text: The PILT Act authorizes regulations on payments by Crown corporations in lieu of real property and business occupancy taxes.
propositions.quote: The PILT Act provides that regulations may be made respecting payments made by Crown corporations in lieu of real property taxes and business occupancy taxes (s. 9(1)(f) and (g)).

propositions.text: Schedules III and IV list federal Crown corporations subject to the Regulations; CBC and MPA appear in Schedule III.
propositions.quote: Finally, Schedules III and IV to the PILT Act list the federal Crown corporations and agents of the federal Crown to which the Regulations apply. The CBC and the MPA appear in Schedule III.

propositions.text: Only corporations in Schedule IV make payments in lieu of business occupancy taxes.
propositions.quote: Only the corporations listed in Schedule IV make payments in lieu of business occupancy taxes.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states the PILT Act's regulatory framework and lists CBC and MPA in Schedule III, noting business occupancy tax payments only by Schedule IV corporations.

propositions.text: The Regulations require Schedule III corporations to pay in lieu of real property taxes and Schedule IV corporations in lieu of business occupancy taxes.
propositions.quote: The Regulations provide that the corporations included in Schedule III of the PILT Act must make payments in lieu of real property taxes (ss. 5 and 6) and that the ones included in Schedule IV must make payments in lieu of business occupancy taxes (ss. 14 and 15).

propositions.text: Payment in lieu must be at least the product of the effective tax rate and property value.
propositions.quote: A payment in lieu of a real property tax must be not less than the product of the effective rate of tax and the property value of the property (s. 7(1)).

propositions.text: Effective rate and property value are those the corporation would consider applicable if property were taxable.
propositions.quote: The Regulations provide that the effective rate or property value is the rate or value that the corporation would consider applicable or attributable to its property if that property were taxable property in the municipality (s. 2).

propositions.text: Disputes about tax rate or property value are referred to the advisory panel under the PILT Act.
propositions.quote: By virtue of s. 12.1 of the Regulations, the procedure for referring a dispute about the tax rate or property value applicable to a property to the advisory panel created under s. 11.1 of the PILT Act also applies to Crown corporations.

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains the Regulations' requirements for payments in lieu, definitions of effective rate and property value, and dispute referral procedures.

propositions.text: Before 2003, CBC and MPA made payments in lieu only for the City's property taxes.
propositions.quote: It is common ground that, prior to 2003, the CBC and the MPA — two corporations included in Schedule III to the PILT Act, but not in Schedule IV — made payments in lieu in respect only of the City’s property taxes.

propositions.text: In 2003, Montréal's municipal taxation structure underwent major changes.
propositions.quote: In 2003, as I mentioned above, major changes were made to Montréal’s municipal taxation structure.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states that before 2003 CBC and MPA paid only property tax PILTs, and that Montréal's tax system changed significantly in 2003.

propositions.text: Before 2003, Montréal imposed property taxes and a business occupancy tax only in some sectors.
propositions.quote: Before 2003, as I have noted, the City imposed property taxes and a business occupancy tax. However, the new City as of that time included several municipalities that had not previously imposed a business occupancy tax. In fact, that tax was collected in only 10 of the City’s 28 sectors.

propositions.text: Business occupancy tax applied to occupants of non-residential immovables engaged in commercial or professional activities.
propositions.quote: Where the tax was in effect, it was imposed on occupants of non‑residential immovables who engaged in commercial or professional activities.

propositions.text: Property tax included a general tax on all taxable immovables plus a surtax on non-residential immovables.
propositions.quote: Moreover, the property tax itself had certain distinctive features. The City first imposed a general property tax on all taxable immovables and then added a surtax on non‑residential immovables.

paragraphs.summary: The Court describes Montréal's pre-2003 tax system, including limited business occupancy tax and a property tax with a surtax on non-residential immovables.

propositions.text: The City reviewed its tax structure to harmonize differing systems and improve efficiency after municipal mergers.
propositions.quote: In light of these disparities, the City concluded that it had to thoroughly review its taxation structure to harmonize the differing tax systems within its territory and improve efficiency.

propositions.text: Quebec legislation authorized municipalities to adopt multiple property tax rates by immovable category from 2000.
propositions.quote: In 2000, the Quebec National Assembly had changed the legislative framework for municipal taxation by enacting legislation that authorized municipalities to adopt between two and five different property tax rates based on the categories to which immovables belonged (Act respecting municipal taxation, R.S.Q., c. F‑2.1, s. 244.29 (added by S.Q. 2000, c. 54, s. 82)).

propositions.text: The amendments allowed municipalities to apply different tax rates to categories like non-residential, multi-dwelling, vacant land, industrial, and residual immovables.
propositions.quote: However, Quebec municipalities could from that time on adjust the tax rate by applying different rates to the various categories of immovables established by the legislation: non‑residential immovables, immovables consisting of six or more dwellings, serviced vacant land, industrial immovables, and immovables that were unclassified and therefore part of the “residual” category (s. 244.30).

propositions.text: The amendments did not change the legal nature of the tax as a property tax on immovables.
propositions.quote: The amendments did not change the legal nature of the tax, which remained a property tax on immovables located within municipalities.

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains the City's tax review and Quebec's 2000 law allowing multiple property tax rates by immovable category without changing tax nature.

propositions.text: In 2003, the City abolished the business occupancy tax and established a variable-rate property tax to recover lost revenue.
propositions.quote: For 2003 and the following fiscal years, it abolished its business occupancy tax and changed its property tax structure. It established a variable‑rate property tax that would enable it, inter alia, to recover the income it would lose after abolishing the business occupancy tax.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states that in 2003 Montréal abolished the business occupancy tax and created a variable-rate property tax to compensate.

propositions.text: The respondents refused to adjust PILTs for tax reforms and argue their discretion allows reducing effective rate by business occupancy tax portion.
propositions.quote: The respondents refused to take account of these reforms in calculating their PILTs. They submit that their effective rate has to be reduced by an amount equivalent to the portion of the property tax increase that corresponds to the amount of the former business occupancy tax.

propositions.text: Respondents argue their exercise of discretion under the PILT Act and Regulations was reasonable.
propositions.quote: In their opinion, they were reasonable in exercising the discretionary decision‑making power they have under the PILT Act and the Regulations where the calculation of their PILTs is concerned.

propositions.text: The City disputes respondents' position and says PILTs were not calculated per statutory and regulatory provisions.
propositions.quote: The City disputes this position and submits that the PILTs were not calculated in accordance with the relevant statutory and regulatory provisions.

propositions.text: The dispute over PILT calculation is central and requires examining the legal nature of respondents' decisions and standard of review.
propositions.quote: This dispute is at the heart of these cases. To resolve it, I will begin by considering the legal nature of the respondents’ decisions and the standard of review applicable to them in the context of an application for judicial review under ss. 18 and 18.1 of the Federal Courts Act .

paragraphs.summary: The Court summarizes the dispute: respondents claim discretion to reduce effective rate, City disagrees, and the Court will examine legal nature and review standard.

propositions.text: Parties debated the scope of respondents' discretion in determining effective tax rates.
propositions.quote: In this Court, the parties engaged in a lively discussion about the nature of the respondents’ decisions regarding the determination of their effective rates of tax.

propositions.text: Appellant argues respondents' discretion is limited in scope.
propositions.quote: The appellant argued that the discretion invoked by the two corporations is limited in scope,

propositions.text: Respondents argue their discretion is broad and gives great latitude in calculating PILTs.
propositions.quote: whereas the corporations argued that it is broad in scope and gives them great latitude in calculating their PILTs.

paragraphs.summary: The Court notes parties' opposing views on the scope of respondents' discretion in determining effective tax rates.

propositions.text: Respondents made decisions under the Regulations involving determining the tax rate for PILT calculation.
propositions.quote: The respondents made their decisions pursuant to the Regulations. The administrative act they are required to perform involves determining what tax rate they will use in calculating their PILTs.

propositions.text: The property value is not in issue; only the tax rate used in PILT calculation is disputed, except for silos in MPA's case.
propositions.quote: The property value of the respondents’ property is not in issue in either case. The respondents are not challenging the values established by the taxing authority, the City of Montréal. Aside from the specific issue of the silos in the MPA’s case, the only point in issue relates to the tax rate to be used in calculating the respondents’ PILTs.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states respondents' decisions concern tax rate determination for PILTs; property value is undisputed except for silos issue.

propositions.text: The Regulations reserve decision-making power to Crown corporations to choose the effective tax rate for their properties.
propositions.quote: As in the PILT Act itself, the Regulations clearly reserve a decision‑making power for Crown corporations. The definition of “effective rate” quoted above refers to the rate that a corporation would consider applicable to an immovable taxed in the municipality if it belonged to a private owner.

propositions.text: Such decisions are discretionary under Canadian administrative law (citing Baker and legal texts).
propositions.quote: In the language of Canadian administrative law, such a decision is considered discretionary (Baker v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [1999] 2 S.C.R. 817, at para. 52; P. Issalys and D. Lemieux, L’action gouvernementale — Précis de droit des institutions administratives (3rd ed. 2009), at p. 63; G. Régimbald, Canadian Administrative Law (2008), at pp. 175‑76).

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds the Regulations grant Crown corporations discretion to choose effective tax rates, a recognized discretionary decision.

propositions.text: Discretion must be exercised within a legal framework and cannot be arbitrary.
propositions.quote: However, in a country founded on the rule of law and in a society governed by principles of legality, discretion cannot be equated with arbitrariness.

propositions.text: Discretionary acts fall within a normative hierarchy defined by statute and regulations.
propositions.quote: Discretionary acts fall within a normative hierarchy. In the instant cases, an administrative authority applies regulations that have been made under an enabling statute.

propositions.text: Statute and regulations define scope and principles governing discretion and allow assessment of reasonableness.
propositions.quote: The statute and regulations define the scope of the discretion and the principles governing the exercise of the discretion, and they make it possible to determine whether it has in fact been exercised reasonably.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states discretion must be exercised legally, within statute and regulations, allowing reasonableness review.

propositions.text: PILT calculation is not mechanical; it upholds federal Crown immunity from taxation and adapts to varying fiscal environments.
propositions.quote: Under the PILT Act and the Regulations, the calculation of PILTs is not limited to a mechanical application of municipal assessments and the tax rates adopted by municipalities. First of all, as I have already mentioned, the PILT Act upholds the principle that the federal Crown is immune from taxation.

propositions.text: Federal Crown and Crown corporations have decision-making power over property and payments in lieu, reflecting Crown immunity.
propositions.quote: The confirmation that the Crown has a decision‑making power in respect of departmental property and that Crown corporations have such a power in respect of the property they manage gives effect to this principle.

propositions.text: Payments in lieu must be adaptable to differing provincial and municipal fiscal and legal environments.
propositions.quote: Next, the system of payments in lieu must be adaptable to a fiscal and legal environment that varies from one province or municipality where federal property is located to another.

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains PILT calculations uphold Crown immunity and must adapt to diverse fiscal and legal environments.

propositions.text: Managers of Crown property must retain discretion due to possible assessment disagreements and property uniqueness.
propositions.quote: There are also practical reasons why managers of Crown property must retain a decision‑making power where the assessment of that property and the tax rates applicable to it are concerned.

propositions.text: Federal properties' diversity and uniqueness can cause technical assessment problems and disagreements with municipalities.
propositions.quote: First, disagreements with taxing authorities about property assessments can occur. As we know, federal properties are very diverse, and can even be quite distinctive, if not unique or almost unique in Canada.

propositions.text: Choosing effective tax rate can be difficult due to property classification and provincial legislation allowing different rates.
propositions.quote: Second, choosing the effective rate of tax may be difficult at times, particularly where the choice depends on how the property is classified and the provincial legislation provides for the possibility of applying different rates depending on the nature of the property involved.

propositions.text: Managers need latitude to protect federal interests if municipalities use taxing powers in bad faith targeting federal property.
propositions.quote: Finally, managers of federal property must retain some latitude so that they can react to protect federal government interests should municipalities use their taxing powers in bad faith to specifically target federal Crown property.

propositions.text: The advisory panel's creation confirms Parliament's intent to safeguard Crown immunity and address disputes.
propositions.quote: The creation of the advisory panel provided for in the PILT Act to resolve this type of dispute confirms that such problems are plausible and that Parliament’s intent was to safeguard the principle that the federal Crown is immune from taxation.

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains practical reasons for Crown property managers' discretion and Parliament's intent to protect Crown immunity.

propositions.text: The existence of discretion means the appropriate standard of review is reasonableness, requiring deference to administrative decisions.
propositions.quote: The conclusion that such a decision‑making power exists resolves the question of the appropriate standard of review. In the instant cases, the appropriate standard is reasonableness, which is particularly suited to reviewing the exercise of a statutory discretion.

propositions.text: Reasonableness review is appropriate for discretionary decisions, showing deference to administrative decision-makers (Khosa).
propositions.quote: Where such a discretion exists, exercising it can lead to the adoption of varying opinions and solutions depending on the application of the relevant legal principles to the facts of the case, and on reviewing a decision of this nature, the court must show deference to the administrative decision‑maker (Khosa, at paras. 59‑60, per Binnie J.).

paragraphs.summary: The Court concludes that discretion calls for reasonableness standard of review, requiring deference to administrative decisions.

propositions.text: Decisions on federal Crown property management involve administrative acts warranting judicial deference.
propositions.quote: The decisions challenged by the appellant relate to the management of federal Crown property. They involve acts of administration in respect of which the courts should, as a general rule, remain deferential.

propositions.text: Judges should not manage Crown property; courts must defer to administrative decision-makers in such matters.
propositions.quote: I readily acknowledge that it is not the role of judges to manage Crown property.

propositions.text: The Court will examine the circumstances and exercise of discretion to determine reasonableness and reviewability.
propositions.quote: In light of this principle, let us now return to the circumstances in which the discretion was exercised and how it was exercised in order to determine whether the respondents’ decisions were reasonable or reviewable by the Federal Court.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states courts should defer on Crown property management decisions and will assess discretion's exercise for reasonableness.

propositions.text: Reasonableness relates to transparency, intelligibility, and quality of reasons and decision outcome.
propositions.quote: The concept of “reasonableness” relates primarily to the transparency and intelligibility of the reasons given for a decision. But it also encompasses a quality requirement that applies to those reasons and to the outcome of the decision‑making process (Dunsmuir, at para. 47); see also, for example, Art Hauser Centre Board Inc. v. Canadian Union of Public Employees, Local 882, 2008 SKCA 121, 311 Sask. R. 272, at para. 33, per Jackson J.A.; Casino Nova Scotia v. Labour Relations Board (N.S.), 2009 NSCA 4, 273 N.S.R. (2d) 370, at para. 30, per Fichaud J.A.

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains reasonableness requires transparent, intelligible, and quality reasons and outcomes.

propositions.text: Transparency and intelligibility of respondents' decisions are not in issue; they explained their basis clearly.
propositions.quote: Neither the transparency nor the intelligibility of the corporations’ decisions is in issue. The respondents made management decisions and clearly explained the basis for those decisions to the City.

propositions.text: Respondents argue they have broad discretion and did not calculate PILTs as City requested after 2003 reforms.
propositions.quote: In substance, they submit that they have a broad discretion under the PILT Act and the Regulations. They did not calculate their PILTs in the manner requested by the City for 2003 or subsequent years.

propositions.text: Respondents argue they must deduct from PILTs amounts equivalent to property tax increase from abolished business tax.
propositions.quote: In their opinion, one result of the reform of Montréal’s municipal taxation system was to have them make PILTs that actually included amounts in lieu of the business occupancy tax. In this situation, the corporations, in fixing the tax rates they considered appropriate, could, and even had to, deduct from their PILTs amounts equivalent to the portion of the property tax increase that resulted from the abolition of the business tax.

propositions.text: MPA considers silos as reservoirs excluded from payment calculations.
propositions.quote: As well, the MPA considered the silos at the port of Montréal to be reservoirs that were excluded from the basis for calculating its payments in lieu.

paragraphs.summary: The Court notes respondents clearly explained their broad discretion and rationale for PILT calculations, including deductions and silos exclusion.

propositions.text: Respondents have discretion but cannot base PILT calculations on a fictitious tax system they arbitrarily created.
propositions.quote: However, there is a fundamental flaw in this interpretation and application of the PILT Act and the Regulations. As I have indicated, the two corporations certainly have a discretion. It is clear from the definition of “effective rate” that Crown corporations have to decide on the appropriate tax rate. However, they cannot base their calculations on a fictitious tax system they themselves have created arbitrarily.

propositions.text: Calculations must be based on the actual tax system existing where the property is located, as if the property were taxable private property.
propositions.quote: On the contrary, those calculations must be based on the tax system that actually exists at the place where the property in question is located. The PILT Act and the Regulations require that the tax rate be calculated as if the federal property were taxable property belonging to a private owner.

propositions.text: Section 2 of the Regulations and PILT Act assume corporations identify the actual municipal tax system to establish property value and effective rate.
propositions.quote: In s. 2 of the Regulations and the corresponding provision of the PILT Act, it is assumed that the corporations begin by identifying the tax system that applies to taxable property in the municipality in order to establish the property value and effective rate of tax.

propositions.text: Corporations cannot base calculations on a tax system that no longer exists.
propositions.quote: They cannot do so on the basis of a system that no longer exists.

paragraphs.summary: The Court concludes respondents have discretion but must base PILT calculations on the actual existing municipal tax system, not a fictitious one.

propositions.text: The business occupancy tax was abolished in 2003 and municipalities can impose variable-rate property taxes under Quebec law.
propositions.quote: The business occupancy tax had been abolished in 2003. Under Quebec municipal legislation, municipalities had the power to impose variable‑rate property taxes.

propositions.text: The City exercised its power to impose variable-rate property taxes after abolition of the business occupancy tax.
propositions.quote: The City exercised that power.

propositions.text: Respondents must calculate effective rates considering the abolition of the business occupancy tax and cannot reintroduce it indefinitely.
propositions.quote: The respondents therefore had to calculate their effective rates having regard to the fact that the business occupancy tax no longer existed. They could not reintroduce that tax in their calculations for an indefinite period of time or indirectly force the municipality to maintain a tax system it had changed as it was authorized to do under provincial law.

propositions.text: Respondents' position would lead to complex, illusory calculations based on long-abolished taxes for many years.
propositions.quote: Indeed, the respondents’ position would in practice mean that they would, in establishing the amounts of their PILTs, be entitled — not only now, but also 10 or 20 years from now — to make increasingly complex and illusory theoretical calculations based on taxes that had long since disappeared.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the business occupancy tax was abolished in 2003, the City imposed variable-rate taxes, and respondents must not reintroduce abolished taxes in calculations.

propositions.text: Respondents' position contradicts the PILT Act's objective to base payments on the existing municipal tax system.
propositions.quote: The respondents’ position is also contrary to the objective of the PILT Act and the Regulations. Parliament intended Crown corporations and managers of federal property to make payments in lieu on the basis of the existing tax system in each municipality, to the extent possible as if they were required to pay tax as owners or occupants.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds respondents' position contradicts the PILT Act's objective to base payments on the existing municipal tax system.

propositions.text: The PILT Act's purpose is fair and equitable administration of payments in lieu of taxes.
propositions.quote: The purpose of this Act is to provide for the fair and equitable administration of payments in lieu of taxes.

propositions.text: The Act confirms federal property tax immunity and voluntary payments but aims for equity and fairness in payments calculation.
propositions.quote: Although the Act confirms both the principle that federal property is immune from taxation and the voluntary nature of payments in lieu, the intention was that the calculation of such payments would be consistent with the objective of equity and fairness in dealing with Canadian municipalities.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the PILT Act aims for fair, equitable payments reflecting federal tax immunity and voluntary nature.

propositions.text: In 1995, a joint technical committee recommended aligning PILT calculations with current property taxation principles.
propositions.quote: In 1995, a joint technical committee made up of representatives of the Federation of Canadian Municipalities, the Treasury Board Secretariat and the Department of Public Works and Government Services Canada considered the question of municipal grants or payments in lieu of taxes. Its report recommended that the calculation of such payments be brought into line with current principles of property taxation: As required by the Municipal Grants Act, the values and rates used to calculate the payments should be those which would apply to federal properties if they were taxable, and should be determined in the context of the assessment and taxation legislation, policies and practices current in the province or territory in question . . . . (Report of the Joint Technical Committee on Payments in Lieu of Taxes, December 28, 1995, at p. 5)

paragraphs.summary: The court notes a 1995 committee recommended PILT calculations align with current property taxation principles.

propositions.text: A 1998 Parliamentary paper stated PILTs should be comparable to local taxes paid by other property owners.
propositions.quote: A Parliamentary paper tabled by the Minister of Public Works and Government Services before the adoption of the current statutory and regulatory scheme expressed the same intention as regards the method for calculating PILTs: The determination of a grant by multiplying the “effective rate” by the “property value” ensures that federal payments in lieu of taxes are comparable in amount to the local taxes paid by other property owners within the municipality.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites a 1998 Parliamentary paper stating PILTs should match local taxes paid by other property owners.

propositions.text: The PILT Act aims to reflect the actual tax situation where federal property is located.
propositions.quote: Thus, the purpose of the PILT Act is to establish a system of payments in lieu that reflects the actual tax situation in the places where federal property is located.

propositions.text: The Department of Public Works calculated PILTs for departmental property in Montréal as proposed by the City, not reducing amounts for the abolished business occupancy tax.
propositions.quote: The evidence shows that the Department of Public Works and Government Services calculated its PILTs for “departmental” property in Montréal as proposed by the City, as it did not reduce the amounts to take the abolition of the business occupancy tax into account.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the PILT Act aims to reflect actual tax situations and the Department calculated PILTs without reducing for abolished taxes.

propositions.text: Respondents' decisions were inconsistent with PILT Act principles and Parliament's intention, leading to unreasonable outcomes.
propositions.quote: The respondents’ decisions were consistent neither with the principles governing the application of the PILT Act and the Regulations nor with Parliament’s intention. The way they exercised their discretion led to an unreasonable outcome that justified the exercise of the Federal Court’s power of judicial review.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds respondents' decisions inconsistent with the PILT Act and Parliament's intention, causing unreasonable outcomes.

propositions.text: Silos are not reservoirs and are used to store dry products, so Parliament did not exclude them from PILT calculations.
propositions.quote: Although silos are containers, they cannot be considered to be reservoirs. They are structures used to store dry plant products, not liquids. Parliament did not see fit to exclude them from the basis for calculating PILTs.

propositions.text: MPA's interpretation of silos is inconsistent with the statute, Parliament's intention, and ordinary meanings, thus unreasonable.
propositions.quote: The MPA’s interpretation is not consistent with the words of the statute, with Parliament’s intention or with any of the ordinary meanings of the words used in Schedule II to the PILT Act. It must therefore be concluded that the MPA’s interpretation is unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds silos are not reservoirs and MPA's interpretation is unreasonable and inconsistent with the statute and Parliament's intention.

propositions.text: The court finds it unnecessary to comment on CBC's cross-appeal as its decision was unreasonable and rejected by the Federal Court of Appeal.
propositions.quote: Moreover, I do not consider it necessary to comment on the CBC’s cross‑appeal. My conclusion that the CBC’s decision was unreasonable suffices to dispose of its cross‑appeal. The solution the CBC advocates — which, moreover, was rejected by the Federal Court of Appeal — is supported neither by the Regulations nor by the tax by‑laws of the City of Montréal.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds CBC's decision unreasonable and rejects its cross-appeal without further comment.

propositions.text: The court allows the appellant's appeals with costs for CBC appeal and without costs for MPA appeal, restoring Federal Court judgments for 2004 MPA year.
propositions.quote: For these reasons, I would allow the appellant's appeals, with costs in the appeal concerning the CBC and without costs in the appeal concerning the MPA. I would restore all the conclusions of the judgments rendered by Martineau J. of the Federal Court, but in respect only of the 2004 taxation year in the case of the MPA.

propositions.text: The court refers matters back to respondents to recalculate payments in lieu of real property taxes.
propositions.quote: I would refer the matters back to the respondents to recalculate the payments they make in lieu of real property taxes.

propositions.text: The court dismisses CBC's cross-appeal with costs.
propositions.quote: I would dismiss the CBC's cross-appeal with costs.

paragraphs.summary: The court allows appellant's appeals, restores Federal Court judgments for 2004 MPA year, refers recalculation, and dismisses CBC's cross-appeal with costs.
